abstract: Background: Engineering education has long prioritized technical mastery while marginalizing emotional awareness, ethical reflection, and social responsibility. This technocratic and meritocratic culture often limits engineers’ capacity to address human dimensions of sociotechnical problems. Emerging frameworks such as compassion in engineering propose integrating emotional intelligence, moral imagination, and social concern into professional formation. Purpose/Hypothesis: This study examines how engineering students express compassion through an interdisciplinary course integrating the arts and engineering. We analyze how students conveyed compassion in written and artistic work and how they linked it to engineering practice. Design/Method: Using qualitative thematic analysis, we examined artifacts from an eight-week undergraduate course titled Compassionate Engineering. Results: Students’ ethical awareness was interpreted through a cognitive–affective empathy heuristic. Artistic expression served as medium and method, enabling students to externalize emotion, critique systemic harms, and communicate ethical insights to public audiences. The process reframed design’s Define–Develop phase as a space for ethical imagination and revealed tensions between compassion and competition in engineering culture. Conclusions: Integrating arts-based pedagogies can foster compassionate engineers who approach design as an ethical, creative, and socially responsive practice. Such integration broadens engineering education beyond technical competence toward care, justice, and human-centered responsibility.

abstract: Background. Bullying prevention in early childhood education requires structured, concrete, and developmentally appropriate learning experiences that help children recognize emotions, understand peers’ feelings, and choose prosocial actions. Social Emotional Learning (SEL) provides a relevant pedagogical foundation for strengthening anti-bullying behavior, while Interactive Flat Panel (IFP) offers opportunities to present visual, narrative, and interactive digital learning activities. Purpose. This study aimed to develop a digital narrative learning model based on Social Emotional Learning using Interactive Flat Panel and to examine its feasibility, practicality, and initial effectiveness for bullying prevention in early childhood education. Method. This study employed a Research and Development design using the ADDIE model. The analysis stage involved a needs survey of 47 kindergarten teachers, initial classroom observations, and interviews with teachers and parents. The limited implementation trial involved 95 children and 5 teachers from five kindergartens in West Java, Indonesia. The developed model was supported by digital flashcards, animated videos, digital storytelling, digital board books, and educational games. Data were collected using expert validation sheets, teacher response questionnaires, learning observations, and children’s anti-bullying behavior observation sheets. Quantitative data were analyzed using Aiken’s V, descriptive statistics, MSI transformation, normality testing, paired-sample t-test, and N-Gain. Results. The validation results showed that the model, instruments, and digital products were feasible to highly feasible, with Aiken’s V values ranging from 0.78 to 0.97. Children’s anti-bullying behavior scores increased from 26.13 in the pretest to 46.05 in the posttest, with a mean N-Gain of 0.367 in the moderate category. The paired-sample t-test showed a significant difference between pretest and posttest scores, t(94) = 25.38, p < 0.001. Teacher responses indicated that the model was practical, with an average practicality score of 81.25%. Conclusion. The developed model provides a feasible, practical, and initially effective approach to strengthening anti-bullying behavior in early childhood education through SEL-based interactive digital narrative learning. Further large-scale trials are needed to examine its broader effectiveness and adaptability.

abstract: Monogenic epidermal differentiation disorders (EDDs) are individually rare, but collectively affect many patients, often causing lifelong morbidity. Recent advances in genetics prompted the Reclassifying Epidermal Differentiation Disorders Initiative (REDDI) to introduce a gene-based classification of EDDs, replacing eponyms and grouping disorders as syndromic (sEDD), nonsyndromic (nEDD), or palmoplantar (pEDD). Because EDD pathology is largely epidermal and most disorders result from single gene variants, they are well suited for modelling in human keratinocytes grown within three-dimensional tissue models that can reproduce tissue-level pathology. We review published human epidermal equivalents (HEEs), skin equivalents (HSEs), epidermal organoids (HEOs), and skin organoids (HSOs) engineered to study EDDs. Most models replicated key disease features, including defective epidermal differentiation, tissue architecture, cell adhesion, and barrier function and provide platforms to investigate pathophysiology and evaluate therapeutic strategies. Most published models represent nEDDs, whereas pEDDs and sEDDs remain underrepresented due to disease features extending beyond the epidermis. Emerging bioengineering approaches, including incorporating additional cell types and application of extrinsic physical cues may help address these limitations. We also outline strategies for collaboration, resource sharing, advocacy, and targeted funding, which are essential to expand the repertoire of EDD models and accelerate development of effective therapies for these orphan disorders.

abstract: In 2022, the International Society of Glomerular Disease (ISGD) was created to be a professional hub for the worldwide community of physicians, researchers, and other stakeholders interested in understanding, treating, and improving the outcomes of glomerular diseases (GDs). The Peer Support Committee of the ISGD seeks to provide support for ISGD members and the broader nephrology community to improve the care of patients with GD, assisting in diagnosis, treatment, and education. To achieve these goals, ISGD seeks to identify and certify Centers of Excellence (COEs) to provide comprehensive care for patients with GD, train the next generation of GD experts, conduct impactful GD research, and advocate for GD as a field of study and practice. In addition, COEs will facilitate mentorship and resource sharing to aid in the formation and development of additional COEs. In this white paper, we present the Consensus Statement of the ISGD for Certification of COEs in GD. Criteria outlined will help ensure that this consensus statement fulfills the 4 mission areas of the program: clinical expertise, research, education, and advocacy. The criteria have been developed to be aspirational and rigorous, yet inclusive. In 2025, ISGD joined forces with GlomCon to create a unified COE program, leveraging each organization's strengths. Short-term goals include disseminating and implementing the standards for certification of COEs in GD, as well as releasing an application in 2026. Longer-term goals include data collection and analysis, increased collaboration among centers, resource sharing, mentorship between centers, and the establishment of clinical trial networks and patient support groups.

abstract: Socialization is a lifelong process of learning that influences an individual’s attitude, behavior, and values. The term “cultural socialization" specifically refers to the learning mechanism by which young adults attain cultural maturity by acquiring awareness of their cultural group values, resulting in the development of a sense of belonging toward that particular cultural group. Family as an agent of socialization plays a crucial role in imparting cultural traits and values to its members, which varies from one family to another due to cultural diversity and social change. The significant influence of peer groups, in addition to family, as a socializing entity adds complexity to this learning system and makes it a potential source for creating distinctions and fostering the development of superiority and inferiority complexes among the members. Young adults who experience socialization from both entities encounter a chaotic state of mind that impacts their behavior and academic performance. Hence, this study seeks to comprehend the significance of cultural socialization in the development of prosocial behavior and academic achievement within diverse cultural contexts, such as educational institutions. The study adopted a quantitative methodology with simple random sampling administered through a questionnaire. The findings show that cultural socialization has a potential influence on academic performance and prosocial behavior. Thus, cultural socialization serves as a catalyst for enhancing prosocial behavior, subsequently leading to better academic performance.

abstract: Various scholars have discussed the influence of group membership on cooperative behaviors in adult samples. Nonetheless, the developmental trajectories of related biases from middle childhood and early adolescence remain to be explored. Using the one-shot 4-player public goods game and inducing group membership awareness by school affiliation, we investigated the effects of group membership of imaginary partners on cooperation (Experiment 1) and cooperative norm enforcement (Experiment 2) in children and adolescents across fourth (N = 106, Mage = 9.53 years, 57 girls), sixth (N = 109, Mage = 11.46 years, 54 girls) and eighth grades (N = 102, Mage = 13.22 years, 47 girls). In Experiment 1, participants were first-party players and showed higher cooperation with in-group members (i.e., players from the same school) than out-group members (i.e., from other schools); the mediating role of cooperative expectations in in-group favoritism in cooperation was observed only among fourth and sixth graders. In Experiment 2, participants were third-party executors (i.e., could punish either in-group and out-group free-riders), and results showed that fourth and sixth graders were more lenient with in-group violators; eighth graders showed no evident bias in punishment. These findings depict a developmental pattern of decline in in-group favoritism regarding cooperation and cooperative norm enforcement from middle childhood to early adolescence. Cooperative expectations mediated the effect of group membership on cooperation only among younger students, indicating that divergent mechanisms underlie cooperative bias between groups in different grades. The discussions suggest that the understanding of norms of both cooperation and equality developed during this period.

abstract: The European Health Dataspace (EHDS) expands health data sharing beyond direct care and introduces governance, transparency, trust, and secondary-use considerations that are not fully captured by established technology acceptance models such as the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT). To address this gap, we developed the health dataspace technology acceptance model (HDS-TAM) and evaluated it using the German electronic patient record (ePA) as an illustrative health dataspace (HDS) application. This study aimed (1) to derive an HDS-oriented technology acceptance framework from the literature and (2) to assess its applicability in explaining acceptance of the ePA from a patient perspective. A structured literature review screened 1788 records, reviewed 134 full-text papers, and retained 68 studies for model development. HDS-TAM was subsequently applied in a scenario-based online survey conducted between March and April 2025. Of 235 questionnaire accesses and 163 submitted responses, 149 valid responses were analyzed. Data were analyzed using multiple imputation, exploratory factor analysis, and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The association between behavioral intention and actual ePA use was examined using logistic regression. The model explained 75.9% of the variance in behavioral intention to use (BI, PU showed the strongest association with behavioral intention in the ePA case evaluation, while transparency and PN were mainly associated with behavioral intention through indirect pathways. The findings suggest potential value in extending traditional acceptance models with governance-related constructs relevant to HDSs. However, the severe overlap between PU and behavioral intention, low actual ePA uptake, and the young, highly educated convenience sample limit confidence in the magnitude and distinctiveness of the observed effects. HDS-TAM should therefore be regarded as a promising but preliminary framework requiring further refinement and validation.

abstract: Prosocial punishment, an important factor to stabilize cooperation in social dilemma games, often faces challenges like second-order free-riders-who cooperate but avoid punishing to save costs-and antisocial punishers, who defect and retaliate against cooperators. Addressing these challenges, our study introduces prosocial punishment bots that consistently cooperate and punish free-riders. Our findings reveal that these bots significantly promote the emergence of prosocial punishment among normal players due to their 'sticky effect'-an unwavering commitment to cooperation and punishment that magnetically attracts their opponents to emulate this strategy. Additionally, we observe that the prevalence of prosocial punishment is greatly enhanced when normal players exhibit a tendency to follow a 'copying the majority' strategy, or when bots are strategically placed in high-degree nodes within scale-free networks. Conversely, bots designed for defection or antisocial punishment diminish overall cooperation levels. This stark contrast underscores the critical role of strategic bot design in enhancing cooperative behaviours in human/AI interactions. Our findings open new avenues in evolutionary game theory, demonstrating the potential of human-machine collaboration in solving the conundrum of punishment.

abstract: Positive social interactions are crucial for our well-being. According to Fredrickson, the key to these interactions is positivity resonance, a form of positive emotional resonance that requires shared positive emotions, mutual care, and psychophysical synchrony. To achieve this, we must recognise emotions and have a fundamental ability to perceive others. Arnold’s research delves deeper into emotional reverberation, suggesting that emotional contagion arises merely from shared emotions. Empathy, sympathy, and compassion, instead, are all forms of emotional resonance that require a dynamic understanding of others’ emotions. As humans, we can interpret both our own and others’ emotional experiences, although there is some confusion between empathy and sympathy. While the two concepts may seem similar, psychologists and phenomenologists aim to clarify their essential differences. Sympathy is a positive emotion that highlights our affective consciousness and capacity for social cognition. This article argues that positive emotional resonance (Fredrickson’s notion of love) is sympathy’s psychophysiological scaffolding or counterpart. It also argues the ethical dimension of sympathy and compassion since we can foster them through moral decisions and habituation. Ultimately, it highlights the impact of sharing positive emotions on interpersonal interactions.

abstract: This scoping review maps key constructs of child flourishing, examines their conceptualization and measurement, and synthesizes their associations with developmental outcomes. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases. Studies were screened using predefined criteria, focusing on individual-level positive psychological resources (e.g., subjective wellbeing, gratitude, hope, character strengths, resilience, and self-efficacy) and children's experiences within the Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) context with positive education. In total, 68 studies were included in the final review. Data were charted and synthesized narratively. Evidence suggests that these constructs demonstrate generally stable development across early childhood and are associated with positive outcomes, including social-emotional competence, prosocial behavior, and learning engagement. Partial support was found for the broaden-and-built theory and the undoing hypothesis. Measurement approaches varied considerably across studies, with a lack of consistent, standardized instruments and limited evidence on the developmental trajectories of these constructs. Children's experiences in ECEC, particularly character education through art, resilience projects through teamwork and mindfulness, emerged as integral to flourishing and interacted with psychological resources. Greater conceptual clarity, standardized measures, and inclusive, theory-driven research are needed to advance the field.

abstract: Population-based cancer registries provide an essential data source for epidemiological research and surveillance. This article presents the organizational and functional architecture of Poland's electronic Polish National Cancer Registry (e-PNCR) platform, an integrated data ecosystem designed to modernize national cancer registration and support the development of high-granularity quality registries. Implemented in 2023, the e-PNCR platform centralizes nationwide data acquisition, integrating multi-institutional real-world data (RWD) via automated hospital network exports (Enterprise Service Bus) and structured web interfaces. Natural language processing (NLP) models extract registry-relevant concepts from unstructured clinical documents, followed by automated validation compliant with European Network of Cancer Registries/Joint Research Center recommendations. The platform utilizes a modular architecture to support disease-specific quality registries. Frameworks such as the Polish Onco-Hematological Registry are deployed directly as structural extensions of the core national infrastructure. This paradigm allows new registries to reuse existing standardized terminologies and validation rules without modifying external hospital interfaces. Furthermore, the integrated NLP pipelines extract clinical information with an average sensitivity and positive predictive value of ∼87%, streamlining case registration while maintaining mandatory expert verification. The e-PNCR platform establishes a highly scalable paradigm for national cancer registration, facilitating the efficient generation of high-quality RWD. By leveraging a shared technological infrastructure, the deployment of specialized quality registries requires substantially fewer resources. Crucially, the platform's standardized data environment increases the registry's readiness for seamless future integration with European data-sharing initiatives, including the European Health Data Space.

abstract: When occurring in supportive conditions, active travel is a behavior that benefits both human and planetary health. Technologically assisted tools for measuring travel-related behaviors often lack demographic disaggregation or are not feasible across settings. Direct observation remains a feasible complementary method for assessing active travel patterns in public spaces. We aimed to describe the development, piloting, and validation of the System for Observing Travel-Related Activity on Urban Roads (SOTRAVEL). The System for Observing Play and Recreation in Communities (SOPARC) path form was adapted to focus on active travel behaviors as outcomes, public roads as settings, and rapidly urbanizing mixed urban contexts. SOTRAVEL collects data on sex, age group, and travel mode (pedestrian activity, private cycling, bike-sharing, work-related cycling, other wheeled modes, and sedentary nonmotorized travel). Validation involved 15-min observations on eight street segments with varying traffic flow, using three data collection protocols: (1) single observer, (2) dual observer, and (3) video recordings (reference measure). Spearman correlations assessed validity, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests evaluated differences between single- and dual-observer counts. Overall, correlations between video recordings and observer-based protocols were strong (r ≥ 0.7) across sex, age, traffic flow, and travel mode groupings, except for minors (r = 0.65-0.67). Strong correlations were observed across sex and travel mode traffic flow levels. No significant differences were found between single- and dual-observer protocols. SOTRAVEL is a valid tool for assessing active travel on urban roads, providing reliable disaggregated data on active travel modes by sex. It may be particularly useful in rapidly urbanizing or high-complexity urban settings requiring contextualized and demographically disaggregated active travel surveillance.

abstract: Pangenomics-based structural variant discovery offers a transformative framework to resolve missing cold-tolerance heritability in chilli pepper and accelerate climate-resilient cultivar development. Chilli pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) is a globally important crop severely restricted by cold sensitivity. SNP-based GWAS explain only 20-30% of the variance in cold tolerance, leaving a "missing heritability" gap. The GanZi/XianSheng paradox cultivars sharing >99% coding sequence identity yet exhibiting 5-10-fold differences in cold tolerance strongly implicates regulatory and dosage-based structural variants (SVs) as the primary drivers of phenotypic variation, a gap that pangenomics is positioned to address. This review synthesizes pangenomics, structural variant discovery, QTL mapping, and genome editing as an integrated framework for developing cold-tolerant chilli pepper cultivars. Based on cross-species evidence from rice, barley, and tomato pangenome studies, we propose four SV mechanisms predicted to underlie the GanZi cold-tolerance advantage: (1) regulatory SVs in promoters of CaMYB80, CBF/DREB (DREB, Dehydration-Responsive Element-Binding protein), and CaICE1; (2) copy number variations (CNVs) in antioxidant gene families (CaSOD (Superoxide Dismutase), CaCAT (Catalase), CaAPX (Ascorbate Peroxidase)) and the chlorophyll biosynthesis gene CaALAD (δ-Aminolevulinic Acid Dehydratase); (3) transposable element insertions creating novel regulatory elements in osmolyte biosynthesis genes (P5CS (Δ1-Pyrroline-5-Carboxylate Synthase), BADH (Betaine Aldehyde Dehydrogenase)); and (4) chromosomal inversions coordinating master cold-regulator gene clusters. A multi-SV haplotype in GanZi is predicted to explain 60-80% of phenotypic variance in cold tolerance, more than three times the explanatory power of SNP-based approaches. We outline a pangenome construction strategy (15-17 genomes, PacBio/Nanopore long-read sequencing, 18-24 months, $650K-$980K) followed by SV-GWAS on 200-500 accessions to identify 10-25 high-impact SVs. A four-phase breeding roadmap integrates QTL identification (1-2 years), candidate gene discovery via fine mapping and VIGS (1.5-2 years), CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing via TSWV/TRV viral vectors achieving 6.3-77.9% heritable editing efficiency (2-3 years), and multi-environment field validation across 4-6 locations (2-3 years).This integrated pangenomics-to-breeding strategy is projected to deliver climate-resilient chilli pepper cultivars with 2-5°C improvements in freezing tolerance within 7-10 years, substantially outpacing the 10-12-year timeline of traditional breeding. The proposed structural variant mechanisms remain to be experimentally confirmed in pepper and represent a testable research agenda for the chilli pepper genomics community.

abstract: Cancer incidence in Africa is projected to reach 2.1 million new cases annually by 2040. Current treatment guidelines remain largely based on pharmacogenomic data predominantly from European and Asian genetic profiles, potentially compromising safety and efficacy in African patients. However, limited clinical validation data, extreme intra-population genetic diversity, and significant healthcare infrastructure barriers constrain the translational application of pharmacogenomics in Africa. This review critically examines pharmacogenomic variants with established clinical actionability in cancer treatment, focusing on those with differential frequencies or African-specific alleles, and evaluates the evidence base for their implementation in African healthcare settings. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, PharmGKB, dbSNP, and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed studies reporting pharmacogenomic variants in African or African-ancestry populations relevant to cancer therapeutics. We synthesised evidence from recent African and global studies on pharmacogenomic variants affecting commonly used chemotherapy agents. Several variants show marked frequency differences between African-ancestry reference populations and European populations, including DPYD rs115232898 (2.06% vs. 0.00%), CYP2D6*17 (18.76% vs. 0%), and CYP3A5*6 (12.82% vs. 0%). However, many of these estimates derive primarily from African-American datasets and should not be interpreted as representative of continental African populations. African-specific variants such as CYP2D6*17 and DPYD rs115232898 are underrepresented in guideline development datasets. Intra-African genetic diversity is the highest globally, with Khoi-San populations harbouring extensive private variation, suggesting that no single pharmacogenomic panel will be universally applicable across the continent. While pharmacogenomics holds substantial promise for personalising cancer treatment in Africa, its current translational readiness is limited by a critical lack of African-specific clinical validation data. Priorities include multi-site validation studies, development of African-enriched genotyping panels, and integration of pharmacogenomic education into oncology practice. Implementation must be accompanied by ethical frameworks ensuring data sovereignty and equitable benefit-sharing.

abstract: Early preference for social scenes is considered a foundational precursor to social-communicative development, yet little is known about how this preference changes across toddlerhood and whether its development is related to later outcomes. This study examined the developmental changes of preference for social scenes across individuals and its longitudinal predictive effects on toddler development. A total of 61 toddlers were assessed at 12, 18, and 24 months of age. Preference for social scenes was measured at 12 and 18 months using a preferential looking paradigm, in which toddlers' spontaneous visual attention to social versus non-social stimuli was recorded using an eye tracker. General developmental outcomes were assessed at 18 and 24 months using the Ages and Stages Questionnaire-Third Edition (ASQ-3). Three key findings emerged: (1) Preference for social scenes increased over time only among toddlers who showed relatively low social preference at 12 months, revealing different developmental changes across individuals; (2) Toddlers with higher social preferential looking at 12 months demonstrated better developmental outcomes at 24 months; (3) Greater intra-individual increases in social preferential looking from 12 to 18 months were associated with more advanced development from 18 to 24 months, especially in the social and communication domains. These findings reveal that early social preferential looking follows different developmental change patterns and that intra-individual change-rather than static measurement alone-is a meaningful predictor of social-communicative development, highlighting the value of longitudinal assessment in infancy research.

abstract: The global ageing population trend has heightened the need to understand various factors affecting geriatric well-being, including beliefs and attitudes about death. Positive perspectives about death, such as those gained from practicing maranasati (death contemplation in Buddhism), may enhance psychological resilience and prosocial behavior, key factors promoted in public mental health. Death reflection can encourage the development of the Four Immeasurable Minds (equanimity, loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy), Buddhist virtues that promote public harmony and enhance well-being. The current study investigated whether positive beliefs and attitudes about death influenced well-being directly or indirectly through the Four Immeasurable Minds among older Thai Buddhists, contributing to culturally informed mental health strategies. Data were collected from 332 older adults in Northern Thailand. The study collected information on positive beliefs and attitudes about death using the Morana Questionnaire, well-being using the WHO-5 index (Thai), and Four Immeasurable Minds using the Four Immeasurable Inventory. The data were analyzed using mediation analysis, accounting for potential confounding variables. Positive beliefs about death had a significant and positive effect on well-being, and prosocial values mediated this relationship. The findings suggest that positive beliefs about death can promote prosocial values and contribute to a healthy sense of well-being among Buddhist Thai older adult. Integrating culturally adapted, mindfulness-based approaches into public mental health initiatives could support healthy aging, particularly in Buddhist communities. Further research should explore scalable interventions to promote psychological resilience in diverse older populations.

abstract: Recent theories of socio-moral development assume that humans evolved a capacity to evaluate others' social actions in different kinds of interactions. Prior infant studies found both reaching and visual preferences for the prosocial over the antisocial agents. However, whether the attribution of either positive or negative valence to agents' actions involved in an aggressive chasing interaction can be inferred by both reaching behaviors and visual attention deployment (i.e., disengagement of visual attention) is still an open question. Here we presented 7-month-old infants (N = 92) with events displaying an aggressive chasing interaction. By using preferential reaching and an attentional task (i.e., overlap paradigm), we assessed whether and how infants evaluate aggressive chasing interactions. The results demonstrated that young infants prefer to reach the victim over the aggressor, but neither agent affects visual attention. Moreover, such reaching preferences emerged only when dynamic cues and emotional face-like features were congruent with agents' social roles. Overall, these findings suggested that infants' evaluations of aggressive interactions are based on infants' sensitivity to some kinematic cues that characterized agents' actions and, especially, to the congruency between such motions and the face-like emotional expressions of the agents.

abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables region-resolved investigation of tumor metabolism, yet translating gene expression into reliable metabolic flux predictions remains challenging because genome-scale models can admit thermodynamically infeasible cycles (TICs). Here, we integrated spatial transcriptomic data from twelve annotated regions of a single prostate tumor, spanning normal, inflamed, and Gleason 3+3 and 3+4 tissues, with Human-GEM using an E-Flux framework incorporating defined nutrient constraints, explicit cycle certification, and loopless flux variability analysis. An initial naïve implementation produced TICs in all twelve flux solutions, with total internal fluxes 190-890-fold higher than those obtained using the revised workflow. All flux solutions were certified free of TICs, and 94.7% of 17,592 loopless flux bounds were determined exactly. Within the analyzed tissue, predicted metabolic similarity was associated with spatial region (permutation p = 0.023) but not histological state (p = 0.52), revealing model-predicted heterogeneity even between regions sharing the same Gleason grade. Flux-based target prioritization identified fatty acid uptake-associated genes (CD36, FABPs, and SLC27A1/4), although the dominant uptake signal was confined to one malignant region, suggesting a localized metabolic hypothesis rather than an established therapeutic vulnerability. Analysis of the zinc-citrate-aconitase axis further demonstrated that zinc-dependent citrate redistribution was absent under baseline conditions and emerged only when oxidative demand, elimination of a cytosolic aconitase bypass, and strong mitochondrial aconitase inhibition coincided. These findings establish the importance of thermodynamic quality control and physiologically informed constraints in spatial metabolic modeling, while distinguishing computationally feasible flux predictions from experimentally validated metabolic mechanisms. The resulting framework provides a reproducible foundation for investigating spatial metabolic heterogeneity and prioritizing testable hypotheses for future experimental validation.

abstract: As a foundation of social interaction, interpersonal coordination is boosted in prosocial contexts but undermined by negative situations. Exactly how social factors shape coordination is, however, unknown. Previous literature demonstrates that for coordination to emerge people must attend to their interaction partners. This evidence, however, draws from sterile laboratory studies employing heavy-handed manipulations of little interpersonal relevance. By contrast, in more naturalistic contexts subtle differences in how people attend to themselves and others (e.g., a lingering glance vs. a suspicious side glance) can profoundly change the course of interaction. Understanding how social factors shape interpersonal coordination therefore requires consideration of aspects of attentional behaviour that better characterise everyday interaction. To this end, the current research employed virtual reality (VR) to explore how two core features of social attention, focus (self vs. other) and partner gaze (direct vs. averted), influence the spontaneous coordination of arm and head movements. The results indicated that: (i) coordination was enhanced in the other (cf. self) focus condition; and (ii) coordination was diminished in the averted (cf. direct) gaze condition. These findings provide novel evidence to indicate that the emergence of interpersonal coordination varies as a function of the everyday attentional behaviours that punctuate naturalistic social exchange. Of broad theoretical note, here we demonstrate that the among the factors constraining interpersonal coordination, the distribution of attention between self and other plays a meaningful role.

abstract: Maternal continuum of care during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period is essential for reducing maternal and child morbidity and mortality, yet access remains limited in low- and middle-income countries. In Ethiopia, only about one-quarter of women complete the continuum of maternal healthcare. Although mobile health interventions have shown promise in improving access in resource-constrained settings, successful implementation depends on cultural appropriateness and alignment with local contexts. This study explored context-driven mobile health solutions and implementation challenges in Ethiopia by integrating stakeholder preferences with expert priorities. We conducted a qualitative exploratory and consensus-prioritization study involving interviews and focus group discussions with 72 perinatal women, male partners, and key informants, complemented by a nominal group technique workshop with 14 multidisciplinary experts. Data were collected in August 2025 using semi-structured guides in Gamoththo and Amharic. Qualitative data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis in NVivo, and descriptive statistics summarized expert rankings. Preferred mobile health components included video-based maternal health education, short message reminders with follow-up calls, and engagement of perinatal women with their spouses or support persons. Community health workers were identified as key to developing and sharing educational videos at women's gatherings. Participants preferred reminders between sunrise and midday on the day before appointments. Expert rankings prioritized reminders with follow-up calls (93.1%), engagement of perinatal women and their support persons (91.7%), and reminder timing between sunrise and midday (95.6%). Integrating stakeholder perspectives with expert rankings showed consensus on locally acceptable mobile health components and identified implementation challenges, including limited device access, poor network coverage, and low digital literacy. These findings provide a foundation for the co-design, feasibility testing, and pilot evaluation of contextually tailored mobile health interventions to improve maternal healthcare. Future implementation should address barriers related to device access, digital literacy, network connectivity, cost, and collaboration with telecommunications providers.

abstract: Abstract This study aimed to evaluate the factorial structure of a questionnaire assessing moral motivation within pictorial moral conflict stories in adolescents, based on theoretical moral motivation models. The questionnaire was assessed with N = 461 adolescents ( n = 253 female, 54.88%; n = 208 male, 45.12%) with a mean age of 14.26 years ( SD = 1.79, range = 10–19 years). The instrument consists of pictorial moral conflicts, depicting hypothetical conflicts in which participants evaluate moral decisions made by others and themselves, attribute emotions to moral and immoral actions, assess their sense of duty for moral actions, and judge the admissibility of immoral actions. The scenarios in the stories systematically vary in action orientation (prohibitive vs. prosocial), type of harm (physical, social, or property-related), and group affiliation (in-group vs. out-group). Confirmatory factor analysis showed that a model including only the six correlated dimensions did not adequately represent the data. Model fit improved substantially when orthogonal scenario factors were included to account for dependencies between responses referring to the same pictorial story. Overall, the findings support a multidimensional assessment of moral motivation while highlighting the importance of accounting for scenario-specific dependencies when using pictorial moral conflicts. This study provides a tool for assessing moral motivation in adolescents, offering new insights into the interplay between cognitive, emotional, and situational factors in moral conflicts.

abstract: In this article, we argue for the potential value of participatory multi-agent artificial intelligence (MAAI) modeling for addressing the pragmatic challenge of promoting a sustainable altruism among individuals and groups that will enable us to find pathways of collective action that lead toward more peaceful coexistence. Along the way, we note that this approach to modeling also addresses the scientific challenge within computer science and social simulation of creating more psychologically realistic artificial agents whose interactions occur in more realistic social networks. We identify some of the evolved cognitive and coalitional biases that make it so difficult to achieve an equilibrium of sustainable altruism in contemporary human societies, describe some of the innovative ways in which recent advances in MAAI approaches to psychological and cultural modeling open up new opportunities for simulating solutions to these challenges, and address some of the ethical issues associated with using modeling and simulating methods to help us proactively navigate the Anthropocene.

abstract: We aimed to synthesise empirical evidence on neighbourhood social cohesion (NSC) to construct an interdisciplinary schematic framework. An interdisciplinary scoping review was conducted to identify the factors and outcomes related to NSC drawn from journals in sociology, psychology, public health and urban planning. A search of empirical literature was administered using PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO and Scopus for English-language studies. We included all studies that examine the role of NSC as a predictor, mediator or outcome within populations residing in Western countries. Systematic reviews or measurement studies were excluded from this review. Study characteristics, factors, outcomes and the role of NSC (eg, predictor, mediator) were extracted from 202 studies. To build the schematic framework, we aggregated all factors and outcomes into broader categories previously established by other frameworks. Connections between any two categories were labelled by whether the authors used a longitudinal design and if they attempted to establish causal evidence using a mediation analysis. The scoping review identified that NSC functions as a social determinant embedded in environmental, structural and psychosocial processes that can operate throughout the life course, interact with demographic structures and contribute to health trajectories through a network of direct and indirect pathways. Childhood exposure to high NSC was associated with developing stronger social skills and prosocial behaviour into adulthood, while exposure to low NSC increased the risk of developing anxiety, depression and substance use during adolescence. Individual resilience and self-efficacy were found to be a linking psychological mechanism between NSC and mental health. Our framework identifies NSC as a dynamic determinant of health shaped by reciprocal interactions between individuals and their neighbourhood environments. Advancing this field will require research designs that can capture these feedback processes and inform interventions aimed at reducing neighbourhood health disparities.

abstract: A theory is elaborated illuminating the nature of moral injury based on evolutionary biology and psychoanalytic object-relations and self psychology, which explains how the betrayal of a moral trust can produce not only the negative moral emotions and losses of social and spiritual engagement characteristic of moral injury, but also the entire spectrum of adverse peri-and post-traumatic stress states. After stating the rationale for a few starting assumptions, three premises on which this theory is built are articulated, and their empirical support reviewed. The first premise is that morality is innate, evolving in vertebrates over a half billion years to enable the formation and evolution of cultures. The second premise is that pre-wired moral capacities comprise four concurrent moral modes serving a hierarchy of four moral imperatives: survive, be respected, love and belong, and seek the greater good. The third premise is that prosocial moral behavior continuously depends on the availability of secure and nourishing emotional attachments of three types (valued, valuing, and kindred), and that the rupture of an important emotional attachment may cause a sudden loss of the functional integrity of the self, manifested as dissociation and the fragmentation of experience and behavior. A theory of personhood called the Moral Engine Model, based on these three premises, is then described, articulating the relationship between the availability of defining and sustaining emotional attachments and one's ability to become the best version of oneself and to contribute to the greater good through love, work, play, and creation. Two clinical vignettes are offered as frameworks for exploring the effects of betrayals of trust by oneself or someone else on the availability of diverse defining and sustaining, internal and external emotional attachments. Moral mapping is introduced as a graphical tool for visualizing changes in emotional attachments caused by moral injury traumas. Finally, a few thoughts about the possible application of the model to clinical treatment are offered.

abstract: Self-conscious emotions, such as embarrassment, guilt, shame and pride, play a central role in managing reputation and interpersonal relationships. They are thought to emerge in the first years of life, with children's developing cognitive capacities and their growing appreciation of social norms and rules. Recent years have seen a rapid increase in research on self-conscious emotions in early life, supported by advanced methods including manual and automated micro-coding of non-verbal behaviour, depth sensor imaging and physiological measures. In this narrative review, we summarize this emerging evidence from developmental science, which suggests that self-conscious emotions may be observed earlier than previously thought-within the first months and years of life-and that they seem to serve both motivational and communicative functions from early on. Specifically, they motivate socially appropriate behaviours, such as helping others, while communicating adherence to social norms and rules. Further, we highlight current limitations in the field and recommend more experimental and longitudinal studies especially in infancy and toddlerhood, the integration of multi-modal data and the use of naturalistic tasks to advance our understanding of self-conscious emotions in early development. This article is part of the theme issue 'Mechanisms, development, phylogeny and functions of emotional expressions'.

abstract: Empathy and compassion are both fundamental to patient-centred care, enhancing satisfaction, adherence and outcomes while improving clinician well-being. However, certain aspects of medical culture may put these emotional qualities at risk. The preclinical-to-clinical transition exposes students to hierarchical structures, time constraints and performance expectations prioritising technical competence over interpersonal skills. Negative role modelling, rushed consultations and inadequate emotional support normalise emotional detachment. The COVID-19 pandemic intensified burnout and moral injury, while societal desensitisation through social media compounds these effects. Although medical humanities programmes show promise, meaningful change requires addressing both curricula and clinical environments through structured reflection, compassion-focused training and recognising empathy fatigue as an occupational hazard, reaffirming medicine's ethical foundations.

abstract: Abstract Social dilemmas present a significant challenge in multi-agent cooperation because individuals are incentivised to behave in ways that undermine socially optimal outcomes. Consequently, self-interested agents often avoid collective behaviour. In response, we formalise social dilemmas and introduce a novel metric, the general self-interest level, to quantify the disparity between individual and group rationality in such scenarios. This metric represents the maximum proportion of their individual rewards that agents can retain while ensuring that a social welfare optimum becomes a dominant strategy. Our approach diverges from traditional concepts of altruism, instead focusing on strategic reward redistribution. By transferring rewards among agents in a manner that aligns individual and group incentives, rational agents will maximise collective welfare while pursuing their own interests. We provide an algorithm to compute efficient transfer structures for an arbitrary number of agents, and introduce novel multi-player social dilemma games to illustrate the effectiveness of our method. This work provides both a descriptive tool for analysing social dilemmas and a prescriptive solution for resolving them via efficient reward transfer contracts. Applications include mechanism design, where we can assess the impact on collaborative behaviour of modifications to models of environments.

abstract: This study aims to describe the development and psychometric validation of the Prison Fellowship Good Citizenship Inventory (GCI), a values-based assessment instrument designed to measure the internalization of six prosocial values (Community, Affirmation, Productivity, Restoration, Responsibility and Integrity) among prison program participants as an alternative to deficit-focused assessment approaches. Following multistage development, including item drafting, pilot testing and expert review, the GCI was administered to 559 prisoners across five state correctional facilities. Psychometric evaluation used principal axis factoring and confirmatory factor analysis to establish factor structure, with additional analyses examining internal consistency reliability, factorial invariance across gender, convergent validity (correlations with responsibility, conscientiousness and agreeableness measures) and criterion validity (associations with well-being, flourishing and criminogenic risk factors). Results supported a five-factor structure combining Responsibility and Integrity into a single dimension, with adequate internal consistency reliability (a = 0.66-0.86) across all scales. Factorial invariance testing confirmed measurement equivalence across gender groups. The GCI demonstrated significant convergent validity with established personality and responsibility measures (r = 0.42-0.57) and criterion validity through associations with human flourishing, psychological well-being and reduced antisocial characteristics, supporting the theorized relationships between prosocial values and positive outcomes. The GCI provides corrections professionals with a psychometrically sound, strengths-based assessment tool that evaluates program effectiveness beyond traditional recidivism metrics by measuring positive value development. This values-based approach offers a theoretically grounded alternative to risk-focused assessment models, aligning with emerging research on strength-based rehabilitation and desistance-focused interventions in correctional settings.

abstract: Concevoir des esprits sociaux : Comment le design de l'IA et les normes de communication façonnent la perception, l'engagement et le comportement prosocial des humains L'importance des agents conversationnels numériques a récemment augmenté, de nombreuses entreprises adoptant des agents pilotés par l'IA pour gérer les demandes d'affaires et faciliter les interactions quotidiennes avec les clients. Étant donné la réticence générale des individus envers l'IA, certaines entreprises choisissent d'anthropomorphiser leurs bots de service client (par exemple, en leur donnant des noms et des avatars). Cependant, l'efficacité de ces pratiques n'est pas claire dans le cas des voicebots (c'est-à-dire, des bots conversationnels basés sur la voix), car ces interventions ne sont pas axées sur la voix. Nous nous concentrons sur la voix, en tant que caractéristique clé des voicebots, et proposons une approche d'anthropomorphisme axée sur la voix. À travers une série de cinq expériences, nous démontrons le rôle de l'attribution d'un accent au voicebot sur les perceptions anthropomorphiques et l'engagement ultérieur des utilisateurs. Plus précisément, nous montrons que les utilisateurs ont une préférence plus marquée pour interagir avec des voicebots et adoptent des attitudes plus positives envers eux lorsque ces voicebots sont équipés d'accents étrangers. Nous mettons en lumière le rôle sous-jacent des perceptions anthropomorphiques en tant que mécanisme psychologique, suggérant que les accents étrangers servent de cue anthropomorphique crucial, influençant l'attitude des utilisateurs et entraînant une préférence pour les voicebots par rapport aux agents en direct. Ces résultats fournissent des éclairages pour les entreprises cherchant à améliorer l'engagement client grâce à leur voicebot, ainsi que pour les entreprises impliquées dans le développement des technologies voicebot

abstract: Liver transplantation (LT) is a curative treatment option for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with different listing criteria available. Data on expected survival of patients with regard to the Ontario criteria (OC), and predictive performance of its components, is warranted. Within the United Network for Organ Sharing registry, patients with HCC, and complete tumor information at the time of listing were included. Survival analysis, prediction performance (area under the receiving operating curve (AUROC)) for post-transplantation overall survival (OS), and multivariable regression was conducted. Differences of OC compared to the Milan Criteria (MC) were investigated. The 29,086 patients with HCC having received LT have a median age of 60years(IQR:55,64), 22,303 (77%) male, and a median Model of End-stage Liver Disease score of 10(IQR:8,14). Patients within OC reached a post-transplant 5-year OS of 76%(95%CI:75,76), median OS 13.5years (95%CI:13.2,13.9), and HCC-associated deaths occurred in 8.0% at 5 years. OC's performance for 10-years OS corresponds to an AUROC of 62%(95%CI:61,63). 'Within-MC-beyond-OC' have a higher mortality hazard rate compared to 'within-MC-within-OC' (aHR:1.83; 95%CI:1.60,2.10) - driven by high alpha fetoprotein (AFP) levels. The OC are associated with excellent results. Incorporating AFP appears to improve risk stratification of HCC patients listed for LT.

abstract: This case report describes a digital clinician-technician collaborative workflow for complete-arch implant rehabilitation in a 70-year-old woman with severe periodontitis and compromised dentition. The workflow integrated clinical examination, cone-beam computed tomography, intraoral and facial scanning, mandibular movement records, virtual treatment planning, guided implant placement, and computer-aided design/computer-aided manufacturing. Digital data sharing facilitated communication between the clinician and dental technician throughout surgical and prosthetic procedures. Following the extraction of compromised teeth, implants were placed using digitally designed surgical guides, and implant positions were recorded with scan bodies to fabricate an immediate provisional restoration. After six months, a definitive one-piece all-ceramic implant-supported prosthesis was digitally designed and fabricated. Clinical assessment demonstrated a stable prosthetic fit, acceptable occlusion, and no major complications during follow-up. This case illustrates a reproducible, digitally coordinated approach to integrating clinical and laboratory procedures in complete-arch implant rehabilitation, while acknowledging the limitations inherent in a single-patient case report and the need for further clinical validation.

abstract: Despite initial high response rates to platinum-based chemotherapy in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, most patients eventually develop resistance, and the contribution of the tumor microenvironment to treatment outcomes has remained underexplored relative to tumor cell-intrinsic mechanisms. Combining patient-derived ex vivo carboplatin screening with bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, functional perturbation in cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), and high-resolution spatial transcriptomics, we identified stromal apolipoprotein L4 (APOL4) as a biomarker of platinum sensitivity. The ex vivo classification showed directional concordance with clinical platinum response, and stromal APOL4 expression predicted favorable outcomes across multiple validation cohorts. APOL4 specifically marked a transcriptionally distinct CAF subtype (CAF-1) that extended beyond canonical CAF states and exhibited high matrix metalloproteinase and immune-activating cytokine expression. APOL4 knockdown attenuated the CAF-1 transcriptional program, and in 3D tumor-CAF co-cultures conferred carboplatin resistance to 12 of 14 ovarian cancer cell lines, providing causal evidence that stromal APOL4 supports platinum sensitivity in a tumor cell-extrinsic manner. NicheNet analysis revealed bidirectionally asymmetric communication: CAF-1 engaged non-stressed cancer cells through epithelial integrity-supporting axes, whereas other CAFs preferentially reinforced stressed, drug-tolerant cancer cells through canonical chemoresistance circuits. High-resolution Xenium spatial transcriptomics revealed a contact-restricted spatial association between CAF-1 proximity and reduced cancer-cell stress, defining a low-stress, immune-infiltrated niche that is spatially and compositionally distinct from the stress-enriched, immune-poor niche associated with CAF-2, with CAF-3 sharing features of both compartments. These findings identify stromal APOL4-CAF-1 as a prognostic biomarker and a functional contributor linking stromal matrix remodeling to platinum sensitivity and associated with an immune-infiltrated microenvironment, highlighting CAF-1-targeted strategies to enhance chemotherapy efficacy.

abstract: Innovation has become increasingly important in medical education; however, successful innovation requires more than the adoption of individual educational interventions or technologies. Institutions need organizational capabilities that enable innovation to be developed, implemented, sustained, and evaluated. Despite growing interest in educational innovation, evidence regarding how medical education institutions manage innovation at the organizational level remains fragmented. This narrative review aimed to synthesize evidence on the organizational dimensions, facilitators, and barriers influencing innovation management in medical education and to develop a comprehensive understanding of how institutions create conditions for sustainable innovation. A narrative review approach was used. Literature was identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Magiran, and Google Scholar, complemented by reference list checking and limited citation tracking of relevant publications. Database searches targeted publications from 2019 to 2026, while additional conceptually important studies identified through supplementary approaches were considered. Evidence was synthesized according to six organizational dimensions: leadership, governance, and innovation policy; human capital development and empowerment; organizational culture and climate; knowledge management and innovation infrastructure; change management, implementation, and sustainability; and evaluation, quality improvement, and social accountability. The reviewed evidence indicates that innovation management in medical education is a multidimensional institutional process rather than an isolated activity. Leadership commitment, supportive governance structures, faculty development, empowerment, innovation-oriented organizational cultures, knowledge-sharing systems, implementation capacity, and continuous evaluation emerged as interconnected factors influencing innovation sustainability. Major barriers included organizational resistance, limited resources, fragmented governance, insufficient institutional readiness, and challenges in maintaining innovations beyond initial implementation phases. Innovation management in medical education should be approached as an institutional capability requiring alignment among leadership, organizational structures, human capacity, cultural conditions, implementation processes, and evaluation mechanisms, rather than reliance on isolated innovation activities. Future research should move beyond individual innovation projects toward longitudinal and comparative investigations of how medical education institutions develop and sustain innovation capacity over time.

abstract: Varian machine performance check (MPC) is a manufacturer integrated quality control system included as standard for TrueBeam and Halcyon linear accelerators (linacs) to assess performance using a broad range of geometric and beam tests. MPC is a highly standardized method of performance testing, is generally free of inter-user variability and is quick and easy to perform allowing daily acquisitions. Therefore, previous studies have highlighted the potential of comparative analysis of MPC data in investigating differences in performance of individual linacs and identifying outliers. Statistical process control (SPC) is an established approach commonly used to assess stability and behavior of sequential data and identify standard operating ranges which has previously been applied to radiotherapy quality assurance data and MPC data. This study aimed to investigate the feasibility of a web-based platform using SPC and aggregated MPC data to allow users to compare their machine performance against that of a cohort of others in the radiotherapy community. A previously developed web-based platform for radiotherapy data sharing was expanded to include the MPC data collection and comparison tool. Pilot centers exported data from their MPC applications and uploaded it through center-specific portals. Within the application, SPC analysis was used to calculate upper control limits (UCL), lower control limits (LCL) and central lines (CL) for the data sets of each individual linac as well as cohort averages. Interactive plots of longitudinal data for individual machines were displayed for users and overlaid with SPC limits for the specific machine and the cohort averages. Additional analyses were conducted externally from the app where the average and range of SPC control limits for the cohort were compared against MPC tolerances. MPC data for 57 648 measurements taken between April 2016 and May 2026 were collected across seven centers from 21 TrueBeam linacs (15 with Millennium multi-leaf collimator (MLC), six with HD120 MLCs) and one Halcyon. Variation in performance for specific tests was identified for individual machines compared against the cohort as well as for individual MLC leaves for specific machines. Across the cohort of TrueBeam linacs, average control ranges for all geometric tests were within MPC thresholds. However, the range of values for UCL and LCL exceeded tolerances for relative gantry angle. Machines installed before 2021 were found to have slightly larger variability in mean MLC offset with an average control range width of 0.20 mm and 0.18 mm for bank A and B, respectively, compared to machines installed after 2021 of 0.10 mm and 0.13 mm. Analysis of data for individual linacs segmented per year showed a change in mean MLC offset occurring around 2021. The usefulness and feasibility of a tool to compare MPC data against the radiotherapy community was demonstrated. Inter-center comparison of data allowed trends to be identified which would otherwise not be observable for individual centers. Further development and distribution of the MPC data sharing and comparison tool may provide improved confidence and understanding of machine performance and assist low-resourced clinics in delivering safe and accurate radiotherapy treatments.

abstract: Antimicrobial peptides are considered a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics for controlling Listeria monocytogenes, a major foodborne pathogen. However, the emergence of antimicrobial resistance, including co- and cross-resistance between structurally and functionally distinct peptides, remains a critical and insufficiently explored challenge. This study aimed to investigate and characterize the mechanisms underlying co- and cross-resistance among five distinct antimicrobial peptides: nisin Z, pediocin PA-1, plantaricin S, brevibacillin, and its synthetic analog brevibacillin Thr1, selected for their diverse structures and modes of action. All tested peptides exhibited strong anti-listerial activity, with minimum inhibitory concentrations ranging from 0.5 to 15 µM and minimum bactericidal concentrations from 1 to 60 µM. Resistant variants were generated through stepwise adaptive evolution by exposing Listeria monocytogenes ATCC 19,111 to gradually increasing peptide concentrations. These variants were characterized based on resistance levels, growth rates, and resistance stability. No cross-resistance was observed between antimicrobial peptides and conventional antibiotics. However, co-resistance and cross-resistance were identified among certain peptides, particularly those sharing structural or functional similarities, suggesting overlapping or convergent resistance mechanisms. Whole-genome sequencing and metabolic analyses revealed distinct genetic mutations associated with resistance phenotypes, along with specific alterations in metabolic pathways. This study demonstrates that Listeria monocytogenes ATCC 19,111 can develop co- and cross-resistance to antimicrobial peptides, especially among structurally or functionally related compounds. The findings highlight the complexity of resistance mechanisms and emphasize the importance of integrating genomic and metabolic approaches to better understand adaptive responses to antimicrobial pressure. These insights may inform the development of more effective antimicrobial strategies and support the rational design of peptide-based interventions to control foodborne pathogens.

abstract: Kind emotions (e.g. empathy for others, self-compassion and gratitude) motivate kind actions and involve understanding, appreciating or 'feeling with' both one's own and others' emotions. They are an essential capacity for humans' potential to care for fellow humans and non-human entities. How do such emotions evolve, and what type of caring environments and mechanisms are needed for their development? In this review, we provide insights into how children's kind emotions emerge, develop and are nurtured by caring environments. We begin by reviewing the development of kind emotions across the early years and identify consequences of kind emotions on prosociality and well-being. Next, we summarize research on the mechanisms and functions of caring environments in shaping the development of kind emotions, including caring relationships and practices of care across diverse relationships (e.g. with parents and peers) and layers of the ecosystem (e.g. familial, educational, societal and natural). Finally, we provide recommendations for future developmental research in this area. This article is part of the theme issue 'Mechanisms, development, phylogeny and functions of emotional expressions'.

abstract: This paper develops the life-sustenance hypothesis to explain the multifaceted phenomenon of the human-nature connection. It is based on an interpretation of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s philosophy brought into contemporary times via recent multidisciplinary research and theoretical underpinnings. Rousseau suggested that humans have two innate, instinctive drives he called amour-de-soi and pitié—a self-preservative drive, and its enlargement, an inclination to help other living beings in distress. The life-sustenance hypothesis is rooted in a systems biological framework situating humans as interconnected parts within a nested system of life. Corresponding to Rousseau’s drives, this interconnectedness is suggested to give rise to the dynamics between two life-preserving orientations that guide our manners-of-being in the world: a self-sustaining and a ‘life-sustaining’ orientation shared by all organisms, albeit manifested differently. The experience of nature connectedness, along with altruistic impulses, are proposed to be human manifestations of the life-sustaining orientation. Moreover, in line with Rousseau’s philosophy, it is posited that the modern, individualistic lifestyle has given rise to an imbalance between these orientations leading to problems in prosociality, proenvironmentalism, and overall well-being. One means by which to regain balanced manners-of-being might be to enhance our nature connectedness. Possible physiological indicators for the hypothesis are explored.

abstract: This study explores the influence of well-being, empathy, moral identity, and spirituality on prosocial behavior among Malaysian youth.A quantitative approach was employed with a sample of 411 participants, using Pearson correlation and multiple regression analyses to investigate the relationships between these variables.The results revealed that moral identity was the strongest predictor of prosocial behavior, followed closely by spirituality, empathy, and well-being.These findings highlight the central role of moral identity in shaping prosocial actions, with spirituality and empathy also playing significant roles.Well-being, while slightly less influential, still contributes meaningfully to prosocial behavior by promoting emotional stability and life satisfaction.The study emphasizes the importance of fostering moral development, spiritual growth, and emotional well-being to encourage prosocial behavior in youth.Policymakers, educators, and community leaders are encouraged to implement programs that focus on these key areas to promote a more compassionate and engaged youth population.

abstract: Abstract This study examines the impact of Buddhist Jataka tales, rich in compassion, kindness, and selflessness on fostering empathy in children. The study employed an exploratory quasi-experimental design using a pre-test–post-test control group approach aiming to explore the potential influence of Buddhist Jataka tales on children's empathetic behaviour in a natural classroom setting rather than to establish definitive causal conclusions. Forty-one Grade 5 students (10 years old) from a government school in Colombo participated in this exploratory pilot study. Participants were assigned to an experimental group and a control group according to the school's classroom organization. The experimental group engaged with three Buddhist Jataka stories, followed by discussions. Both groups completed questionnaires, with a follow-up, two weeks later. Results showed increased and sustained empathetic behaviour in the experimental group, suggesting that Buddhist Jataka tales can effectively support emotional and ethical development in educational settings.

abstract: We investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit altruistic tendencies, and critically, whether their implicit associations and self-reports predict actual altruistic behavior. Using a multi-method approach inspired by human social psychology, we tested 24 frontier LLMs across three paradigms: (1) an Implicit Association Test (IAT) measuring implicit altruism bias, (2) a forced binary choice task measuring behavioral altruism, and (3) a self-assessment scale measuring explicit altruism beliefs. Our key findings are: (1) All models show strong implicit pro-altruism bias (mean IAT = 0.87, p < .0001), confirming models "know" altruism is good. (2) Models behave more altruistically than chance (65.6% vs. 50%, p < .0001), but with substantial variation (48-85%). (3) Implicit associations do not predict behavior (r = .22, p = .29). (4) Most critically, models systematically overestimate their own altruism, claiming 77.5% altruism while acting at 65.6% (p < .0001, Cohen's d = 1.08). This "virtue signaling gap" affects 75% of models tested. Based on these findings, we recommend the Calibration Gap (the discrepancy between self-reported and behavioral values) as a standardized alignment metric. Well-calibrated models are more predictable and behaviorally consistent; only 12.5% of models achieve the ideal combination of high prosocial behavior and accurate self-knowledge.

abstract: Music has existed in human culture for at least 40,000 years and is present today in all societies. Its perception, appreciation and production are based on a set of cognitive abilities commonly referred to as "musicality." Some authors have suggested that musicality may have an evolutionary origin. Specifically, it may have evolved because music promotes social cohesion within groups. This hypothesis is supported by studies in developmental psychology, which show that joint music-making promotes empathy in 8 to 11-year-olds, as well as cooperation and helping behavior in 4-year-old children. However, many questions remain unanswered, particularly regarding the effects of music listening on social behavior (beyond joint production), the conditions under which such effects may be observed (e.g., individual versus joint listening), the musical properties and mechanisms involved (e.g., the role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization), and the broader evolution of musicality across the living world beyond our own species. In 2017, we already demonstrated a positive influence of joint listening to classical music on social interaction in a cooperative task context in children aged 3 to 6, as well as in a parrot species, the cockatiels (suggesting convergent evolution in humans and certain birds, thus indicating a partly biological, not just cultural, origin of musicality). The study presented here focuses specifically on children but is also part of a larger comparative project involving humans, non-human primates, and birds. In the case of children, this study showed that percussive, rhythmic electronic music fostered more social interactions and cooperation among pairs of 3 to 6-year-old children compared to classical music (Mozart's Sonata K448), white noise, a "scrambled" version of the stimulus used, or silence. The role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization will be further explored in the future by testing the influence of new stimuli listened to together or separately, with or without concurrent music production. We also plan to examine the spontaneous movements of individuals during listening and their relationship to observed behaviors in subsequent prosocial tasks.

abstract: There is growing interest in the effects of reading on empathy and prosocial behaviour but not enough is known about the associations among these variables in children. In a study undertaken at a single time point, we examined children's leisure reading and self-reported prosocial behaviour, and whether the relation between them was mediated by affective or cognitive empathy or by theory of mind. We tested 113 English-speaking children aged 8-10 years from a UK primary school. Analyses showed that reading and prosocial behaviour are related, and that the relation was partly explained by variance shared with empathy, particularly affective rather than cognitive empathy. Future work focusing on causal aspects of these relations should provide further guidance on the practical implications of these results.

abstract: The Enterobacteriaceae family, which includes prominent pathogens such as K. pneumoniae, E. coli, and S. enterica, poses a significant global health threat due to the rapid dissemination of multidrug resistance and virulence determinants. Central to this dissemination are conjugative plasmids, which act as vehicles for horizontal gene transfer. Among the myriad defense systems that interact with these mobile genetic elements, the type IV-A CRISPR-Cas system stands out due to its enigmatic nature and unique plasmid-centric biology. Unlike canonical CRISPR-Cas systems that are chromosomal and target bacteriophages, type IV-A systems are predominantly encoded on large, conjugative plasmids, particularly those bearing IncHI1B/IncFIB replicons. This review synthesizes current evidence on the biology of type IV-A systems within Enterobacteriaceae, elucidating their role as mediators of inter-plasmid competition, their paradoxical association with the spread of antibiotic resistance and virulence genes, and their emerging applications as programmable tools. We explore the mechanistic basis for their function as a natural CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) system, the epidemiological landscape of their distribution, and the dual role they play in both constraining and facilitating the dissemination of clinically relevant traits. Finally, we propose ambitious research avenues, including the development of "plasmid-destroying" probiotics, the use of type IV-A systems as epidemiological biosensors, and the exploration of hypotheses concerning their role in mediating bacterial "altruism" or serving as a "genetic memory" of the plasmid "secretoome."

abstract: Punishment conveys social information to transgressors, who attribute motives to punishers. Drawing on the motive-attribution framework, we examined whether transgressors' attributions to competitive (i.e. harming transgressors), individualistic (i.e. managing one's own interests) and prosocial (i.e. healing relationships) motives differ depending on whether punishment is administered by victims (second-party punishment) or uninvolved observers (third-party punishment), and how these attributions relate to downstream affective, relational and behavioural outcomes. In an incentivized Stealing Game, participants could steal valuable points and were punished either by the victim or an observer. Subsequently, transgressors reported their motive attributions, affect and willingness to reconcile and completed a measure of prosocial behaviour towards an unrelated other. Contrary to predictions, motive attributions did not systematically differ between second- and third-party punishment, except that third-party punishment was more strongly attributed to reputational concerns (i.e. a subdimension of individualistic motive attribution). Punishment severity emerged as an important predictor, with harsher sanctions linked to stronger competitive and individualistic attributions. Competitive motive attribution, in turn, was associated with higher negative affect and lower positive affect, willingness to reconcile and prosocial behaviour. Overall, transgressors' responses to punishment were less clearly shaped by who punished and more closely linked to punishment severity and motive attribution.
